newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti port privatization could face protests.
newsitem.headline: Haiti port privatization could face protests.

text.p: Plans to privatise Haiti's national port under a controversial government reform programme could run into squalls of protest, Haitian officials say.
The National Port (ANP), which brings in at least $25 million a year to the national budget, is the most expensive in the Caribbean, its director Julio Julien told Reuters.
A cargo boat can pay up to $60,000 to dock there for two days.
Julein said the port was in need of complete renovation and reduction of the workforce to make it competitive, pointing to a neighbouring facility built by Haitian businessman Fritz Mevs.
"Everything needs to be improved here. Mevs is about 50 per cent cheaper," Julien said.

The government plans to privatise nine state-run enterprises including the port, airport, telephone and electricty companies, through joint ventures, management contracts and concessions. Studies on how best to carry out the plan are being made under World Bank guidance.
Planners say the reforms will bring more jobs for Haiti, where unemployment is running at 70 percent, but many workers fear jobs will actually be lost.

"Everyone down at APN gets scared when you mention privatisation because they know they can lose their jobs. But those workers will not stay quiet, they will rally the population when it comes time," said a maritime agent working at the port, who asked not to be named.
"The privatisation of the port is impossible, just wait and see," he added.

While the port struggles with a bloated workforce and an outdated system, Mevs, whose port lies just down the bay next to the City Soleil slum, has fuel lines to transport gas, 14 storage tanks and cheaper prices that are more attractive to cargo boats.
During the U.S.-led intervention against a military junta in 1993, the U.S. military stored fuel and other items at Mevs' port, providing him with the revenue to expand.
"Mevs made a lot of money off of the U.S. because when they came they did not care how much money they spent, they were just glad to have the access," a U.S. official said.
Other U.S. officials said they did not see the port as a threat to privatisation.

Brian Atwood, administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development who visited Haiti last week, said that although he was unaware of the private port, most goods would come through the national port.

Atwood signed an agreement with the Haitian government during his visit to provide Haiti with $30 million in food aid under a programme called PL-480, which gives flour and wheat to the administration to sell on the local market.
But all of the PL-480 aid will come through the Mevs port according to Julien.
"Now he is a competitor and the guy is powerful," he said.
Others see the competition as healthy.
"It's the sign of a normal functioning society," parliamentarian Litz Felix said.
